title: Arts and culture operate as social infrastructure, but cost and welcome determine who can convert participation into belonging
source_unit: Canadian Heritage and Canada Council for the Arts, Arts and Heritage Access and Availability Survey 2025-26, conducted by Leger
geography: Canada; national survey of residents ages 16 and older, including a telephone sample from the territories

observations.period: 2025-26 survey; in-person and online cultural participation

denominator.unit: Canadians surveyed: 5,000 primarily online plus 150 telephone respondents from the territories

in_person_attendance.unit: percent reporting attendance at an arts or culture performance or event in person during the prior 12 months

online_participation.unit: percent reporting online arts or culture participation during the prior 12 months

increased_in_person_since_before_pandemi.unit: percent reporting increased in-person engagement compared with before the pandemic

increased_online_since_before_pandemic.unit: percent reporting increased online engagement compared with before the pandemic

participation_pattern.value: Cultural participation is both a live social practice and a digital practice, with neither mode representing the whole cultural public

observations.method: Canadian Heritage and Canada Council survey conducted by Leger, primarily online with a territorial telephone supplement; national descriptive estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The sample is not a longitudinal panel, the modes differ, and reported participation is subject to recall, nonresponse, and access-to-internet differences; increased engagement is self-reported.
observations.subgroup: Canadians ages 16 and older, including residents of the territories; the public page reports national participation totals rather than a full subgroup table.
observations.counterinterpretation: High participation can reflect occasional attendance rather than durable cultural involvement, while online participation may complement rather than substitute for live social connection.

observations.period: 2025-26 survey; motivations and barriers to in-person cultural attendance

denominator.unit: Canadians who attended at least one arts or culture event in person; published page reports qualitative ranking rather than a single sample count

primary_motivations.value: Enjoyment and socializing with friends or family were the main motivations for attending in person

leading_barrier.value: Cost was the leading barrier to participation

mechanism.value: Cultural participation can create social connection, but household budget room determines whether that infrastructure is reachable

observations.method: Survey description of reported motivations and barriers among respondents, as summarized by Canadian Heritage and the Canada Council for the Arts.
observations.uncertainty: The public summary does not provide the full distribution, effect sizes, or causal relationship between price and nonattendance; cost may interact with transportation, time, caregiving, geography, and perceived welcome.
observations.subgroup: Respondents who attended or considered attending arts and culture events; the public page does not publish a complete demographic breakdown for this result.
observations.counterinterpretation: Cost may be the leading stated barrier while free, community, digital, or informal cultural practices remain available; nonattendance is not equivalent to cultural isolation.

observations.period: 2025-26 survey; perceived quality of life, community, and national belonging

denominator.unit: Canadians surveyed in the national access and availability survey

quality_of_life_importance.unit: percent saying arts or culture performances and events are important to their quality of life

community_better_place.unit: percent saying arts and culture make communities better places to live

local_economy_importance.unit: percent saying arts and culture are important for local economies

cross_cultural_connection.unit: percent agreeing arts and culture help bring people together across different languages and cultures

mechanism.value: Respondents attach civic, economic, and social value to culture, but stated collective value does not by itself demonstrate equal access or actual cohesion outcomes

observations.method: Weighted national survey estimates as summarized by the sponsoring public cultural agencies.
observations.uncertainty: These are attitudes and perceived benefits, not experimental estimates of cultural participation causing community cohesion, local economic growth, or belonging.
observations.subgroup: Canadians ages 16 and older; the public summary presents national estimates without full subgroup intersections.
observations.counterinterpretation: People may endorse the social value of culture without attending events themselves, and cultural venues can be valued while remaining financially, geographically, or socially exclusionary.

observations.period: 2025-26 survey; cultural organizations as participation and contribution infrastructure

denominator.unit: Canadians surveyed in the national access and availability survey

support_or_contribution.unit: percent reporting donation of money, goods, or services, purchase or renewal of a membership or subscription, or volunteering with an arts or culture organization

welcome_in_cultural_facilities.unit: percent saying they feel welcome in cultural facilities

local_community_belonging.unit: percent saying arts and culture help them feel part of their local community

national_belonging.unit: percent saying arts and culture help them feel part of Canada

mechanism.value: Cultural infrastructure has a contribution route beyond attendance, but welcome and belonging are lower than broad claims about cultural social value

observations.method: Survey estimates of cultural-organization support, perceived welcome, and belonging reported by Canadian Heritage and the Canada Council for the Arts.
observations.uncertainty: The bundled contribution measure combines different behaviors, and perceived welcome or belonging is subjective; the survey does not establish whether organizations caused these feelings.
observations.subgroup: Canadians ages 16 and older, including cultural participants, supporters, members, subscribers, and volunteers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Membership, donation, volunteering, and purchase behavior may be concentrated among already-engaged publics; cultural institutions may support belonging for some while reproducing barriers for others.

related_sources.claim: Canadian government publication route for the survey report.
U.S. NEA comparative research route on arts participation and civic/community engagement.

boundary: This record adds a comparative cultural-infrastructure route from arts access through socializing, local and national belonging, perceived community value, and organizational contribution while preserving cost and welcome as access conditions. It is a national survey summary, not a causal evaluation, a measure of actual cohesion, a longitudinal participation panel, or proof that cultural institutions distribute belonging equally.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Canada Council for the Arts publication page was reviewed for sample, methods, participation, motivations, cost barriers, perceived cultural value, welcome, belonging, and contribution measures.
